opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we think about constantly, because in embodied AI it's easy to get excited about impressive demos that never become products.

For us, the starting point is the market, not the technology. We ask: where is there real, repeated demand that today's labor supply struggles to meet, and where the task structure is regular enough that a robot can perform reliably? Retail, pharmacies, and warehouse logistics stood out early. Picking items from shelves, restocking, moving totes. These tasks happen thousands of times a day, the value of automating them is clear, and the environment is semi-structured. It isn't a fully controlled factory line, but it isn't a chaotic home kitchen either.

Then we look at the skill itself through a few lenses.

First, generalization. Can one skill cover a huge variety of objects? Grasping is a good example. If we can grasp tens of thousands of different SKUs — boxes, bottles, soft packages, transparent items — without per-object engineering, that one capability unlocks a lot of commercial scenarios. Something extremely specialized, like threading a particular cable, may look impressive but transfers poorly.

Second, data feasibility. Our approach relies heavily on large-scale synthetic data and simulation, then transferring to the real world. So we favor skills we can simulate with good enough fidelity: rigid-body grasping, placing, opening drawers and doors. Highly deformable manipulation, like folding clothes, is fascinating research, but the sim-to-real gap is much larger, so it's harder to make commercially robust right now.

Third, reliability requirements. A customer doesn't care that you succeed 80% of the time in a lab. They care whether the robot works all day without someone babysitting it. So we choose skills where we believe we can reach very high success rates, and where failure is recoverable. If the robot misses a grasp, it can try again. That's very different from a task where one mistake breaks something or creates a safety risk.

And finally, composability. We want skills that act like building blocks: navigate, perceive, grasp, place, open, close. Chained together, they form complete workflows. That's how you go from a single-skill demo to something that actually replaces a full job function.

So it's a balance: commercial demand pulls us toward certain tasks, and technical maturity — especially whether we can generate enough high-quality data — tells us which ones we can deliver now and which belong on the roadmap. The goal is to ship something useful today while each deployment pushes the general capability forward.

r001.rationale: It advocates selecting commercially demanded, reliable, broadly useful skills and describes combining core capabilities into workflows that deliver commercial value.

r002.rationale: It does not propose having people perform less critical tasks while robot capabilities are being developed.

r003.rationale: It does not identify hidden human choreography as a source of robots’ apparent abilities in filmed demonstrations.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question we think about constantly, because you can't do everything at once. The way I frame it is: which skills unlock the largest number of real tasks with the smallest increase in system complexity?

Grasping is the obvious starting point, because almost every useful task begins with picking something up. But "grasping" in a lab and grasping in the real world are very different things. In the lab you have a clean table, known objects, good lighting. In a home or a warehouse you have clutter, transparent objects, deformable bags, things partially hidden behind other things. So the first filter is generalization: a skill is only worth building if we can make it work across thousands of object categories and environments we've never seen, not just a benchmark set.

The second filter is frequency. We look at what people actually do, hour by hour, in the environments where a robot would be deployed. Pick and place, opening and closing things, pouring, wiping, handing objects to people. Those few categories cover a surprisingly large share of real activity. A very impressive skill like threading a needle or tying shoelaces is a great demo, but it rarely shows up in a day's work, so it's a lower priority.

The third filter is data. A skill is commercially viable only if we can collect or synthesize enough data to make it robust. This is why I'm a big believer in simulation and large-scale synthetic data for the foundational skills, and then using real-world data to close the gap. If a skill requires months of expensive teleoperation for every new scenario, it won't scale.

And the last thing is safety and failure cost. Early on, we favor tasks where a mistake is cheap. Dropping a box is fine. Dropping a glass of hot water near a person is not. So the order we develop skills in is partly determined by where the robot is allowed to be imperfect.

Put those together and you get a roadmap: general grasping first, then dexterous and bimanual manipulation, then longer-horizon tasks that chain those primitives. The goal is a small set of broadly generalizable capabilities, rather than a long list of narrow tricks.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes a small set of broadly generalizable, high-frequency skills for commercial viability.

r002.rationale: It does not propose having people perform less critical tasks while robot capabilities are developing.

r003.rationale: It does not mention behind-the-scenes human choreography in filmed demonstrations.

astra-6.text:
I would start with the application, rather than with a list of skills. What task does the customer need done, how often does it happen, and what does it cost them today? Then you can work backward to the manipulation capabilities the robot actually needs.

For example, picking up an object is only one part of a useful workflow. The robot may need to identify it, grasp it without damage, place it accurately, and recover if something goes wrong. A successful demonstration doesn’t tell you whether that whole process is reliable enough to make economic sense.

So I would prioritize skills that unlock a valuable end-to-end task, with clear requirements for speed, reliability, and hardware cost. And among those skills, I’d favor ones that transfer across objects and settings. That gives you a focused commercial starting point while building capabilities you can reuse as you expand.

r001.rationale: It recommends focusing on skills that enable a valuable end-to-end commercial task and calls this a focused commercial starting point.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest having people perform less critical manipulation tasks while robot capabilities are being developed.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute robots’ apparent abilities in filmed demonstrations to behind-the-scenes human choreography.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the application, rather than with a particular manipulation skill. Who is the customer, what task do they need done, and what would make a robot useful enough that they would pay for it? Then you work backward to the capabilities you need.

For example, picking up an object is not a complete commercial task. The robot may also need to find it in clutter, move it without damaging it, place it accurately, and recover when something goes wrong. So I would prioritize the skills that let the robot complete that whole workflow reliably.

There is also a balance between value and difficulty. A task might be very valuable, but if it requires extraordinary dexterity in an unpredictable environment, it may be a poor first product. I would look for a task with real demand, enough repetition to justify automation, and a manageable range of variation. Start there, make the system dependable, and use what you learn to expand into more tasks.

r001.rationale: It says to start with the customer’s task, work backward to needed capabilities, and prioritize skills that make the full workflow reliable.

r002.rationale: It does not propose having people perform less critical manipulation tasks while robot capabilities are being developed.

r003.rationale: It does not mention behind-the-scenes human choreography or filmed demonstrations.
